title: Dropped Name
passages:
Dawn bled pale across Anza's ore stub, the kind of light that shows every crack in the rail ties and every oil stain on the concrete. The blank rig was already a shrinking coal on the northbound line, its hand lamp a wobbling orange eye retreating toward the Blank. No transponder pulse. No board entry. Just eleven warm canisters and a flame in a crew box window, rolling north on stolen momentum.

Kass walked the empty siding with their boots kicking up rail dust, the pedal-rail shed yawning dark behind them. Anza's chain had gone green again at 08:00 — Teodoro's trick with Voss's name — but the node still tasted like held breath. Clearances stripped. Resupply frozen until the re-list took. Nour's chalk still held forty names under an amber chain that hadn't been amber since morning.

A flash of white in the gray dust. Kass stopped, boot heel grinding it flat.

A coast ticket. Heavy card stock, folded sharp into thirds the way you fold something you mean to keep. The bought name on the face meant nothing — *J. RENNER, TRANSIT CLASS, VALID THROUGH WINTER* — but the graphite thumbprint smudged into the corner, and the deep crease from a coat pocket's hard edge: those were Miko's. Kass had watched Miko fold tickets that way a dozen times. Pocket, unfold, check, pocket. The rhythm of someone who didn't trust anything to stay put.

Kass picked it up with two fingers, turned it over. Blank back. No stamp. No punch. If the ticket was here, its owner wasn't. And Miko had three of these things under three different names, paid for with cargo weight Kass didn't want to know about.

The wind shifted, carrying the rig's diesel ghost south. The hand lamp bobbed once, steady as a breath held.

Kass slipped the ticket into their own pocket, coat crease matching coat crease, and kept walking the siding toward the pedal-rail shed. The ore line stretched north, empty and patient. Culvert Nine sat penciled on Anza's board in Saul's careful hand — proposed, not live. A dead pump station with a live storeroom and a woman who'd marked it in her own name.

Kass's badge caught the light, thin and bent at one corner. They had a tally card cleared, a glove with a cut palm, and a chip match made but not read out. They had a thread they wouldn't drop.

The pedal-rail waited in its shed, chain dry, bearing ready to shriek. Past the first node, there was no one left to call.
